doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Founding the Jazz Museum in Harlem with Garment's million dollars
summary: Opening offices in 2001-02, restricted federal funding, board members Marsalis and Burns, Appelbaum design.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: amount of money. In terms of building a 501C3 and creating an organization in New York City it’s like $10 and that’s a crazy thing to say but that’s the truth. I mean if you’re looking at something major. Plus the money came with all kinds of restrictions. Couldn’t use it for fundraising, could only use it for the salaries and for research and stuff like that. Well we opened up an office in Harlem and we decided that we needed to aim big so that the genius, the great quality that Len had at that time was, even though we had nothing to show except a desk and a telephone and a board of directors or something like that, he said, “You know what, we’re going to shoot big.” We’re going to build a big museum and we’re going to hire the best people, and even though we didn’t have the money to do that, ‘cause this million dollars, trust me, was going, it was going with this and with that. We’re going to hire the best people, and so we had articles in the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal because of who Len Garment was, for the great aspirations of this organization. And so, let me think of how I can collapse this so it makes sense. I brought Wynton Marsalis and Ken Burns on board. I’d been working with Wynton at Jazz at Lincoln Center just as a consultant or as an educator and I had participated as one of the consultants on the Ken Burns Jazz series. So they agreed to join the board, even though we didn’t have anything, and it was a great thing for Wynton because of course he has his own organization that he has to raise money for. So people started saying well, you’ve got these great plans, I had written the NPR Curious Listeners’ Guide to Jazz in 2001. We took that book and with a lot of other opinions created an exhibit model for the museum for a 50,000 square foot museum. We hired a guy named Ralph Appelbaum, who designed the Clinton Library and the Civil Rights Museum and paid him a huge chunk of that money that we had gotten and spent two years designing what a 50,000 square foot museum would look like. The exhibits, the this, who would be in the exhibits, what the, all the interstitial stuff and this kind of stuff. In the meantime people started saying but what are you actually doing? You’re planning but what the hell are you doing? I can’t give money to an organization that’s planning to be big someday. So we started doing public programming. And that became the tail that wagged the dog or whatever that expression is. It just started almost as an afterthought and it became who we are and who we still are. Oral histories, hundreds of them, with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar or Bobby Short or Roy Haynes or Clark Terry or Chico Hamilton or Billy Taylor, or just I mean name all the people. But also significantly, the lesser known people.
